text: A model nobody can understand or reproduce is a liability. Six months from now, a colleague, or you, will ask what data trained this, how good is it, and what shouldn't I use it for. Documentation answers those questions before anyone has to ask, and the numbers should come from code, not memory.

Every project ships four documents. A README explains what it is and how to run it. A model card explains what the trained model is, its data, its numbers, its limits. A decisions log records why you chose what you chose. And requirements.txt pins the exact library versions.

A good model card states a purpose and a non-purpose: rank churn risk, not price or credit decisions. It reports results by segment, not just on average, because a model that's good overall can be poor for one group. And it lists limitations a reader can actually check.

Fill the template from code with Python's str dot format, which raises a key error if a fact is missing, a useful safety net. We ran the whole script twice and got byte-for-byte identical output, including a twelve-character fingerprint, a short hash of the data. If a colleague's fingerprint differs from yours, you are not looking at the same data.

On the churn model from lesson 21, the rendered card reads: four thousand customers, a twenty-seven point two percent positive rate, test ROC AUC zero point eight oh two, recall zero point four four seven. Broken out by contract: month-to-month scores zero point seven seven five, one-year zero point seven six two, two-year zero point seven nine. Those segment numbers are what a plain average would hide.

Set random_state everywhere and write the seed in the card. Freeze the environment with pip freeze. Save the fitted pipeline with joblib dot dump, and record the scikit-learn version it's tied to. Keep the card beside the model file, and log each real decision while you still remember why you made it.

Good limitations are specific and checkable, like threshold zero point five misses most churners, not vague lines like results may vary. Stating limits is what makes a reviewer trust the rest. Next: the capstone, where you'll document your own project this way.
